title: Even water counts in the MRT
text: That MRT entrance? Don't even think about finishing your water bottle down there. Sipping plain water past the gates can get you fined NT$1,500 to NT$7,500. The official worry is crumbs luring insects that chew cables and mess with the automation. In Tokyo, meanwhile, the rulebook just says: eat if you must, don't bother others.

title: The softer flashing green
text: That blinking walk man got a softer job description since this March. If you haven't stepped off the curb yet, you're now told to avoid entering, not prohibited from entering — which effectively removes the old NT$500 fine. In Japan the rule is the same — flashing means wait like a yellow — except the light is officially called blue, not green.

title: Orange YouBikes' Xinyi start
text: Those chunky orange bikes parked on every corner started life as a tiny 2009 trial in Xinyi. The city still runs the system together with Giant Bicycles, so the hardware is solid local stock. In Tokyo, for example, the docks look different — mostly docomo bike share and HELLO CYCLING rigs.

title: Convenience store forest
text: Bet that 7-Eleven across the street has another one practically waving at it from the next block. Taiwan counted about one convenience store for every 1,659 people in 2025, with 14,236 stores island-wide. In Japan it was about one per 2,180 people, so you're walking through an even denser forest of midnight snacks.

title: Scooters Off the Arcade
text: That covered arcade along the shopfronts was meant as your sidewalk. Back in 1999 Taipei started shooing scooters off these walkways to give them back to walkers. So if this stretch feels oddly strollable for scooter-central, that's why — enjoy the cover while the rain decides what to do.

title: Rooftop water tubs
text: Those chunky grey tubs crowning the roofs up here? They're commonly explained as a buffer for outages and wobbly pressure. Word is a one-ton tank keeps a family of four going for a day or so. Japan has similar gravity-fed rooftop tanks too, though some cities now push direct supply.
